overview.title: The process at a glance
overview.text: Seven canonical stages. Modes – Independent Expert, Adversarial Review, Consensus – change how the council is orchestrated, not just the wording.
overview.gateText: Approve, select an alternative, request more debate, request changes or reject. Proposals with a critical security objection cannot be approved.

phase.independent_thinking: Every model receives the identical brief and answers blind. No model sees another proposal before the reveal.
phase.open_council: All proposals are revealed side by side. Models ask each other precise questions and answer them.
phase.twelve_minds_council: Up to twelve perspectives – architecture, security, cost, critic and more – review every proposal.
phase.minority_review: Dissent is first-class. Substantiated objections are checked by independent models and may stay unresolved.
phase.consensus_round: Authors revise their proposals against the objections. Agreements and open disagreements are documented.
phase.final_verdict: Independent scores, hard gates and a separate majority vote produce a reproducible verdict – then you decide.
phase.execution_council: Optional, with a connected GitHub repository: after your approval a task plan, sandboxed code, tests, reviews and a draft pull request.

byok.title: Your keys. Your providers.
byok.text: CONSYRION AI is bring-your-own-key only. You connect your own API keys and pay the providers directly – CONSYRION AI sells no AI credits and has no fallback key.
byok.p1: Keys are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before they are stored and are never shown again.
byok.p2: Each key is checked against the provider; model lists come live from the provider.
byok.p3: Every session has a hard token budget that is enforced on the server.

delivery.title: Your decision, where you work
delivery.text: Most teams need the reasoned decision, not code. Take the verdict as a report or into your tools – a pull request is one option, only with a connected repository.

story.title: How CONSYRION AI works – from your question to a reasoned decision
story.example: Example scenario – illustration, not live data.

top.title: Debate. Decide. Deliver.
top.text: Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Kimi and other AI models think independently, challenge each other and reach a documented verdict with evidence. You approve – and take the decision where you work: as a report, in your tools or, with a connected GitHub repository, as a reviewed pull request.

prepare.title: Your question becomes a brief
prepare.text: Create a project and describe the decision. Choose the models and up to twelve perspectives. You connect your own provider keys and set a hard token budget – CONSYRION AI sells no AI credits.
prepare.example: Question: “Which database architecture should our SaaS product use?” – three models, twelve perspectives, a budget on your own keys.
points: Your own API keys, your budget

independent-thinking.text: Every model receives the identical brief and works on its own. Answers stay sealed until all are in – no model can see or copy another.
independent-thinking.example: Model A drafts a managed multi-tenant database, B a self-hosted cluster, C a hybrid – none of them sees the others.

open-council.text: All proposals are revealed at once and laid out side by side as equals. You compare the alternatives while the models ask each other precise questions.
open-council.example: Side by side: A is fastest to launch, B gives the most control, C balances both. B asks A how tenants are kept apart.

twelve-minds.text: Roles such as architecture, security, cost and critic unfold around the models and test every proposal. Twelve perspectives are roles – not twelve extra models or votes.
twelve-minds.example: The security role checks tenant isolation, the cost role compares running costs, the critic looks for weak spots.

minority-review.text: A substantiated objection is highlighted and checked against evidence by independent models. Dissent is recorded – never smoothed away.
minority-review.example: One objection stands out: in A, a misconfiguration could let tenants see each other’s data. Evidence: test results and provider docs.

consensus-round.text: Authors revise their proposals against the objections; compatible ideas can merge into a hybrid option. Differences that remain stay documented.
consensus-round.example: A adds per-tenant keys and merges with C into “Hybrid A + C”. B’s cost concern stays documented.

final-verdict.text: Recommendation, independent scores, evidence and the minority position come together in one decision report. Nothing is built at this point.
final-verdict.example: Recommendation: Hybrid A + C – with scores for security, cost and time to launch, and the security objection on record.

approval.title: You decide
approval.text: Approve, choose an alternative, ask for more debate, request changes or reject. A proposal with an open critical security objection cannot be approved. Without your approval nothing is built.
approval.example: You approve Hybrid A + C – or ask for one more round on cost first.

build.text: Only if you want it and a GitHub repository is connected: after your approval the decision becomes tasks, code, tests and independent reviews – delivered as a draft pull request. Most decisions need no build; merge and deployment stay your separate decisions.
build.example: Tasks: schema, per-tenant keys, migration tests – opened as a draft pull request in your repository.

start.title: From your question to a reasoned decision – delivered where you work, optionally all the way to reviewed code.
start.text: Your keys, your providers, your approval. Every step leaves evidence you can follow.

cruxes.title: Key disputes
cruxes.intro: The disagreements that decided this verdict or still threaten it – each one from stored council events.
cruxes.revisedMoot: Yes – v{version} no longer contains what was criticised
cruxes.remaining: Still open after the Consensus Round
cruxes.source: Shown as stored: claims, answers and reviews are model statements, not a fact check. Full history: tab Minority Review & Consensus Round.

dashboard.approvableYes: {n, plural, one {# proposal can be approved} other {# proposals can be approved}}
dashboard.nothingBuilt: Nothing is built before you decide. These are model judgements with reasons, not a fact check.

outcome.no_qualifying_solution: None of the proposals meets the requirements
outcome.provisional: Provisional favourite – limited review, not approvable
outcome.conflict: No solution can meet these requirements

facts.title: Review facts
facts.openRequirements: Requirement checks not met or open
facts.note: Counted from stored checks; ! marks what limits the verdict.

overall.title: Overall score
overall.intro: Weighted mean of the independent evaluations, 0–10. A proposal that misses a requirement cannot win on points.

dashboard.barAria: Proposal {label}: {score} of 10{blocked, select, yes {, not approvable} other {}}
dashboard.evaluations: {n, plural, one {# independent evaluation} other {# independent evaluations}}

criteriaCard.title: Strengths per criterion
criteriaCard.intro: Mean score per criterion (0–10) and its weight in the overall score.
criteriaCard.legend: Highlighted: highest value per criterion among approvable proposals. Lock = not approvable.

requirements.title: Hard requirements
requirements.intro: Each requirement against each proposal, as the independent evaluators judged it. Click a cell for every evaluator's reason.

cell.noChecks: No stored check for this cell.
cell.note: Stored model statements, not a fact check.

objections.title: Open objections
objections.intro: Accepted or undecided objections from the Minority Review, by severity. Objections a revision made obsolete are not counted.

table.caption: Scores 0–10 per proposal and criterion (weight in brackets).

dashboard.allBlocked: All {n} proposals are not approvable – the scores show quality, not a winner.

agreement.title: How far the evaluators agree
agreement.intro: Each dot is one independent evaluator's raw score (0–10) for this proposal; the line is the server's mean. Hover a dot for its reason.
agreement.note: A spread of 3 or more points (!) means the models judge this criterion very differently – read their reasons.
agreement.none: No independent scores are stored for this proposal.

tokens.title: Tokens per model
tokens.intro: All council calls on your own API keys (build calls: tab Execution Council).
tokens.failed: {n, plural, one {# failed call} other {# failed calls}}

nextSteps.title: Next steps
nextSteps.introRecommended: For the recommended Proposal {label}: what to check first, what to test, when to stop and when to ask the council again.
nextSteps.introLeading: No proposal can be approved yet. For the best-scored Proposal {label}: what is missing and what to check before deciding.

verify.title: Settle before any irreversible step
verify.source: Unconfirmed requirements and open objections from the council
verify.empty: Nothing open – every requirement confirmed, no open objection.

assumptions.title: Riskiest assumptions – test these first
assumptions.source: The author's own assumptions, as written

stopIf.title: Stop and re-check if …
stopIf.source: High and critical risks the author named
stopIf.empty: Not specified – no high or critical risk named.

revisit.title: Ask the council again when …
revisit.source: Points the Consensus Round left open
revisit.empty: Not specified – no open disagreement recorded.
revisit.pointer: New facts on one of the {n, plural, one {# open point} other {# open points}} listed under “Key disputes”.

nextSteps.note: Built from stored council statements only, nothing generated. A test plan stays a plan: it does not confirm a requirement, and nothing is built or started without your decision.
nextSteps.introChosen: For Proposal {label}, which you chose: what to check before an irreversible step, what to test, when to stop and when to ask the council again.
nextSteps.introTie: There is no single recommendation (the leading proposals are too close). For the best-scored Proposal {label}: what to check before you choose.

roleSuggestion.title: Suggested perspectives for this project
roleSuggestion.intro: From your brief and confirmed requirements – no model call. Apply it or keep your own choice.

always.security: Always suggested: a security and downside check belongs in every council.
always.critic: Always suggested: an independent critic looks for what the others miss.

roleSuggestion.notSuggestedWhy: no matching topic in the brief or the requirements. You can still activate them below.
roleSuggestion.note: Perspectives are not extra votes: majorities and independent reviews are counted per model.

questions.software_architect: Does the structure carry the requirements and later growth?
questions.security_expert: What can go wrong – data, access, abuse – and how is it prevented?
questions.performance_engineer: Is it fast enough under real load, and where is the bottleneck?
questions.backend_engineer: Are the server parts, APIs and jobs sound and testable?
questions.frontend_engineer: Can users actually work with it, on every screen size?
questions.database_architect: Do the data model, queries and migrations hold up?
questions.devops_engineer: How is it deployed, monitored, backed up and recovered?
questions.cost_analyst: What does it cost to build and to run, and is that within budget?
questions.product_strategist: Does it solve the right problem for the users and the market?
questions.quality_assurance_expert: How is it proven to work, and what would break unnoticed?
questions.maintainability_reviewer: Will the team still understand and change it in a year?
questions.independent_critical_thinker: What is everyone else overlooking – is there a simpler or safer way?
